title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage

severity.usersAffected: Nationwide — the majority of South Korea's population relies on KakaoTalk; ~2M users reported to have left the app in the immediate aftermath (single-source, low confidence)
severity.impactUsd: Over KRW 2 trillion in Kakao-affiliate market-cap loss on Oct 17 (single-source, low confidence); Kakao committed KRW 460B (~US$323M) to new Ansan capacity

brief: On 15 October 2022, a lithium-ion UPS battery on the third basement level (B3) of the SK C&C Pangyo Data Center ignited and spread, forcing firefighters and operators to cut power to the entire facility. Because tenant Kakao had concentrated core functions — including its sole authentication service — at this single site, the power cut cascaded into a nationwide outage of KakaoTalk, Daum, Kakao-linked banking, KakaoT and dozens of downstream services. Co-tenant Naver, which kept its own separate data center, was far less affected. KakaoTalk stayed down for more than 11 hours, the longest in its history, and full restoration of all Kakao services took roughly five days. The event triggered a CEO resignation, a three-way blame dispute, and South Korea's "Kakao Outage Prevention Act" mandating geographic redundancy for major platforms.

magnitude.note: Blast radius and user impact are at ceiling: KakaoTalk is de-facto national communications infrastructure, and the outage propagated into banking, ride-hailing, deliveries and grocery. Duration scores high on the 5-day-plus full-restoration tail (7,650 min ≈ 127.5 h) even though the headline KakaoTalk downtime was ~11 hours. Financial score reflects the reported >KRW 2 trillion affiliate market-cap loss (low-confidence, single-source) plus the KRW 460B remediation commitment.

sequenceOfEvents.event: Fire ignites in the lithium-ion batteries of a UPS system in the B3 (third basement) battery room and spreads to the rest of the building.

Power to the facility is cut to enable firefighting. Kakao — single-homed at this site — loses nearly all services; co-tenant Naver, backed by its own separate data center and off-site backups, sustains or restores most services within hours.
Firefighting escalates: 114 firefighters and 46 units of equipment are mobilized. Gas fire extinguishers prove ineffective against the li-ion cells, which keep heating the UPS.
Kakao publicly predicts restoration 'within two hours' of power resumption.
Kakao announces recovery delays due to ongoing power issues.
Kakao states power cannot be immediately supplied for safety reasons.
Partial Daum News service is restored — the first meaningful service recovery.
Some KakaoTalk message send/receive functionality is restored, roughly 11 hours after onset.
Text messaging (excluding photos/videos) normalizes in general chat.
Photo/video transmission fails again amid recurring instability during the staged bring-up.
Most of Kakao's main services are restored to normal operation.
Brunch and Kakao Map web normalize (long-tail services).
Kakao Pay securities and real-estate services restored.
Kakao declares all services fully restored — a total of 5 days, 7 hours, 30 minutes (~127.5 h) from onset.

rootCause:
TRIGGER. On 15 October 2022 at approximately 15:30 KST (오후 3시30분경), a fire broke out in the basement electrical room of SK C&C's Pangyo data center in Seongnam, South Korea. The Korean-language record states the ignition point as "지하 3층 무정전전원장치에서 발화" (ignition in the UPS at basement level 3, B3F), and ZDNet Korea's same-day report independently places the origin in the underground electrical room ("지하에 위치한 전기실에 발생한 것으로 알려졌다"). The seat of the fire was thus the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) / battery installation on the B3F electrical floor — the very equipment meant to provide backup ride-through power.

MECHANISM — WHY THE OUTAGE HAPPENED WITHOUT SERVERS BURNING. Critically, the fire did not physically destroy the tenant server halls. ZDNet Korea confirms the fire did not spread to the server/computer rooms ("화재가 서버실과 전산실까지 확산되지 않아"). The outage was instead caused by a deliberate fire-safety measure: to prevent the fire from spreading and to allow firefighters to work safely around energized electrical equipment, power to the entire building was cut ("건물 전체 전원 공급을 차단"). This building-wide de-energization — not flame or smoke damage to compute hardware — is what took the servers offline. On-site UPS/battery redundancy could not bridge the load because the UPS installation itself was the seat of the fire and the whole building was intentionally de-energized. (The frequently cited "~15:29 power cut to Kakao's zone" is not supported by the retrieved sources and is omitted here.)

WHY REDUNDANCY DID NOT ABSORB THE LOSS. The loss of a single facility should, in a properly distributed architecture, have been survivable via geographically dispersed failover. The Korean record identifies the core organizational root cause as the absence of an effective distributed data-center architecture: the facility operated as a single point of failure and Kakao's servers were insufficiently dispersed. The record is pointed that nothing had changed since a materially similar single-data-center-dependency outage a decade earlier (April 2012): "10년 전 사건이 일어났을 때 이후로 서버 분산 등의 달라진 점이 없다." Because a critical share of Kakao's core services (and other tenants including Naver) was concentrated in this one center without working cross-site failover, the single-facility power loss cascaded into a nationwide service outage.

ESCALATION AND SLOW RECOVERY. The fire was suppressed the same night at 23:46 KST, 8 hours 13 minutes after ignition ("8시간 13분 후인 그날 23시 46분에 진화되었다"). Restoring power nonetheless proved slow because the fire-damaged electrical room could not be safely re-energized immediately. Recovery therefore stretched far beyond suppression: mobile KakaoTalk was partially restored overnight, but full service restoration was not completed until 20 October 2022 ("10월 20일 23시, 모든 서비스와 기능들이 복구 완료됐다") — roughly 127 hours after the fire, one of the longest outages in the company's history. MSIT (과학기술정보통신부) coordinated the government response and Kakao co-CEO Namkoong Whon resigned over the outage (confirmed by the English Wikipedia Kakao article: "co-CEO Namkoong Whon resigned after a service outage caused by a data center fire").

SOURCING CAVEAT (unchanged and important). The B3F-UPS ignition finding and the "power-cut, not fire-damage" mechanism are drawn from ZDNet Korea (same-day) and Korean/English Wikipedia aggregations — press/tertiary sources, not a primary forensic document. The verbatim MSIT official cause-investigation report (reported published 2022-12-06) and any NFS/police final forensic conclusion (in particular whether the precise battery-ignition mechanism was conclusively determined or left undetermined) were NOT independently retrieved. The specific attribution of the forensic origin investigation to the NFS (국립과학수사연구원) and the Gyeonggi Nambu Provincial Police is not supported by the retrieved sources and should be treated as unverified. The exact ignition mechanism inside the UPS/battery installation therefore remains reported-but-not-primary-verified.

Official confirmation. Official source genuinely established this pass. The MSIT investigation press release ('디지털서비스 장애 원인 조사결과 및 시정조치 요구', 6 Dec 2022) was read via korea.kr, the official Korean-government policy-briefing portal (KOGL type-1) that republishes MSIT releases verbatim — a legitimate primary official/regulatory document, hence officialPostmortem=true. MSIT's own msit.go.kr served a maintenance/bot-block page for every request, so the ministry-hosted copy could not be read directly. The fire-origin conclusion comes from the National Forensic Service (NFS) 감정 결과 and the police+NFS+fire-authority joint on-site exam; these are official-body findings but were only accessible as verbatim Yonhap wire quotations (labeled 'press' here for honesty), since NFS/police did not publish standalone public reports. The exact reason for the battery cell's internal insulation breakdown remained officially undetermined and no criminal charges were filed as of the reporting. There was no prior detailed root cause supplied; the finalRootCause was constructed from the official findings.
contributingFactors: Single point of failure / no effective geographic redundancy: Kakao concentrated a critical share of its core services in the one Pangyo facility without a working distributed data-center architecture or live cross-site failover, so a single-site power loss became a nationwide outage (ko.wikipedia).

Repeat of a known, previously-realized risk: a materially similar single-data-center-dependency outage had already occurred in April 2012, and the record notes nothing changed in server dispersion in the decade since — '10년 전 사건이 일어났을 때 이후로 서버 분산 등의 달라진 점이 없다' (ko.wikipedia).

Co-location of the fire's ignition source with the facility power path: the fire started in the B3F UPS/battery installation itself, so the very equipment meant to provide backup/ride-through power was the seat of the fire, negating on-site UPS redundancy (ko.wikipedia; ZDNet Korea corroborates the basement electrical room).

Fire-safety response required total building de-energization: to suppress the fire safely, power to the entire building was cut ('건물 전체 전원 공급을 차단'), so an electrical-room fire that never reached the servers ('화재가 서버실과 전산실까지 확산되지 않아') still took all tenant compute offline (ZDNet Korea).

Slow, safety-constrained power restoration: even after suppression completed at 23:46 the same night ('8시간 13분 후인 그날 23시 46분에 진화'), the fire-damaged electrical room could not be safely re-energized quickly, extending full recovery to Oct 20 23:00 (~127 hours) (ko.wikipedia).

lessonsLearnt: Fire-suppression design must match the fuel: gas-based extinguishers are ineffective against lithium-ion thermal runaway, so battery rooms need physical separation from critical power equipment and suppression rated for li-ion.

Single-site concentration of a mandatory dependency (here, the sole authentication service) turns a facility incident into a total-service outage — no amount of intra-DC redundancy substitutes for geographic redundancy; the same fire left redundancy-holding co-tenant Naver largely functional.
A total power cut-off is a plausible and catastrophic failure mode; disaster-recovery planning must assume the loss of an entire data center, not just individual components.
Recovery estimates given to the public should be conservative; Kakao's '2 hours' prediction was overtaken repeatedly and eroded trust as the outage stretched past 11 hours.
Fire-response protocols are worthless without rehearsal — the absence of detailed action plans and fire drills materially worsened SK C&C's response.
Effective incident response depends on clear information-sharing with emergency services; poor coordination with firefighters slowed containment.
improvements: Physically separate lithium-ion battery banks from UPS and IT power equipment, with dedicated li-ion-rated detection and suppression.
Establish true geographic redundancy for core services, with special priority for single-points-of-failure such as authentication/verification.
Implement and regularly drill a facility-loss disaster-recovery runbook that assumes full power cut-off.
Strengthen battery-management, monitoring and early fire-detection instrumentation to catch thermal runaway before ignition.
Formalize emergency-response protocols with detailed, rehearsed action plans and structured information-sharing channels with firefighters.
Stage service bring-up on validated infrastructure to avoid the recurring instability seen when partially recovered systems were reloaded.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The incident began as a battery-room fire: lithium-ion cells in a UPS system on the B3 basement level entered thermal runaway and ignited, then spread through the building. Critically, the batteries were not physically isolated from the UPS, so the facility's gas fire-suppression system could not extinguish the reaction — the cells kept generating heat and re-feeding the fire. With suppression defeated and a spreading blaze in a live electrical room, the only safe option was to cut power to the entire facility, converting a localized fire into a complete loss of the data center.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why it cascaded nationally
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The blast radius was set not by the fire but by architecture. Kakao had concentrated core functions at this single Pangyo site, including its sole authentication/verification service. When the site went dark there was no geographic failover, so nearly every dependent Kakao service — KakaoTalk, Daum, KakaoT, Kakao Pay, and many Kakao-auth-dependent banking and payment functions — was disrupted at once, and downstream sectors that had built on Kakao (banking, ride-hailing, deliveries, grocery) were hit with them. Co-tenant Naver, by contrast, kept most of its services running by failing over to its own separate data center — the same fire, opposite outcome, determined almost entirely by redundancy. A facility incident thus became a de-facto national-infrastructure outage affecting most of the population.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Recovery dynamics
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Recovery was slow and non-linear. Power could not be safely restored quickly, so Kakao's early '2-hour' estimate slipped through a sequence of delay announcements on Oct 15. Restoration proceeded in stages: partial Daum News by 23:21, first KakaoTalk text by 02:16 Oct 16 (~11 hours in), then a server bring-up from 12,000 to 27,000 of 32,000 servers across Oct 16. The staged bring-up on partially recovered infrastructure produced fresh instability — photo/video transmission failed again at 10:15 — and long-tail services (Brunch, Kakao Map, securities/real-estate) trickled back over the following days, with full restoration declared only at 23:00 on Oct 20, a total of 5 days 7.5 hours (~127.5 h).

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The ICT ministry assigned blame across all three stakeholders. SK C&C was faulted for a sketchy fire-response protocol with no action plans or drills, weak battery monitoring and fire detection, and poor information-sharing with firefighters. Kakao was faulted for concentrating core functions at one site. The accountability fallout included a CEO-level resignation at Kakao and multiple lawsuits, plus a public blame dispute: SK Group — whose subsidiary SK On supplied the batteries and whose affiliate SK C&C operated the facility — denied responsibility, citing its battery-management-system records. The regulatory response was forceful — one-month deadlines for emergency-response plans, ordered fire drills, and a national push toward resilient-services guidelines and the Kakao Outage Prevention Act mandating geographic redundancy.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This incident sits squarely in a recurring class of failures where a physical-plant event (fire, power) exposes a latent architectural single point of failure. The technical trigger — lithium-ion energy storage that resists conventional suppression and forces a full power cut — is a known and rising risk as li-ion displaces VRLA in data-center UPS fleets. The amplification pattern — one facility, one authentication dependency, no geographic failover — mirrors other national-scale platform outages where concentration, not the initial fault, determined severity, and the sharply better outcome for redundancy-holding Naver in the very same building makes the point concrete. The regulatory outcome (mandated redundancy) reflects a broader trend of treating dominant consumer platforms as critical infrastructure subject to resilience law.

technicalDeepDive:
At the facility electrical layer, the ignition originated in the B3F electrical room's UPS / battery installation ("지하 3층 무정전전원장치에서 발화"). A data-center UPS room houses the battery energy store and power-conversion equipment meant to bridge the load during a utility interruption and deliver clean power to downstream server halls. Because the fire was in this power-infrastructure room rather than the compute halls, the servers themselves were not burned — ZDNet Korea confirms the fire did not reach the server/computer rooms ("화재가 서버실과 전산실까지 확산되지 않아"). The failure therefore propagated through the power path, not through thermal damage to IT equipment.

The decisive engineering event was the intentional building-wide power cut ("건물 전체 전원 공급을 차단"). Fighting a fire in an energized electrical room with water is hazardous, so responders de-energized the whole building, removing power to every tenant rack simultaneously. On-site ride-through (UPS batteries) could not carry the load: the UPS/battery installation was itself the fire origin, and a whole-building de-energization for firefighting overrides any single-room battery backup. The result was a facility-scoped, total power loss to compute. (No retrieved source substantiates a specific ~15:29 power-cut timestamp for Kakao's zone, so it is not asserted here.)

At the service-resilience layer, the blast radius was governed by architecture, not the fire's physical extent. With a properly distributed active-active or active-passive multi-site design, loss of one facility's power should trigger automated failover to another region within seconds to minutes. The Korean record indicates this was not in place — the facility was a single point of failure, Kakao's servers were insufficiently dispersed, and server distribution had not changed since the comparable 2012 incident. Consequently the single-facility power loss propagated to a nationwide, multi-day service failure.

At the recovery layer, suppression at 23:46 KST ("8시간 13분 후") did not enable immediate restoration: a fire-damaged electrical room cannot be safely re-energized until inspected and cleared, so server power stayed down or came back only gradually, with full service restoration at Oct 20 23:00 (~127 hours). The binding constraint on recovery was safe re-energization of damaged power infrastructure plus the manual, non-failed-over rebuild of services — not the fire duration itself.

Note: the precise ignition mechanism inside the UPS/battery installation (a definitive lithium-ion thermal-runaway determination vs. an undetermined electrical fault) is reported via secondary aggregators; the primary NFS/MSIT forensic documents were not directly verified in this reconstruction, and the specific NFS/Gyeonggi-Nambu-Police attribution is unverified.
